newsitem.title: FINLAND: FINNISH SAK SAYS PLANS TO CUT LOW WAGES RECKLESS.
newsitem.headline: FINNISH SAK SAYS PLANS TO CUT LOW WAGES RECKLESS.

text.p: Chairman Lauri Ihalainen of the Central Organisation of Finnish Trade Unions (SAK) on Wednesday called a proposal to cut low-wage earners' nominal salaries as part of a programme to create new jobs reckless and unrealistic.
"It is a reckless proposal, which has no realistic foundation whatsoever. Minimum wages are already now too low to live off and there is no reason to reduce nominal wages," Ihalainen told reporters.
"The underlying idea ... that tax cuts would be targetted at those with low or medium income, is correct," Ihalainen added.

Ihalainen sits on the economic council -- an informal discussion forum led by the prime minister and made up of key cabinet ministers, the central bank governor, trade union and employer confederation leaders and heads of big business lobbies.
On Wednesday morning, the council discussed a report by a group of senior economists, who proposed that income taxes should be cut by about nine billion markka in 1998-99.
But they also said big income tax cuts for low-wage earners should pave the way for lower nominal wages for unskilled workers and so give employers more incentives to hire new staff.

The report said the disposable income of employees earning less than 6,500 markka per month (the mean Finnish monthly salary is around 10,500 markka) would rise by 1,500 markka per month if they didn't have to pay income tax at all.
Such an income tax cut would benefit employers in the form of lower pay rise demands, the report said.
"If the tax relief affected only low-wage earners, the reflection on labour costs would require a freeze or cut in minimum wages in several sectors," it said.

Tuire Santamaki-Vuori, head of research at the Labour Institute for Economic Research -- an institute close to the largely social democratic trade union movement led by SAK, was one member of the economist group behind the report.

The economists also said earnings-related jobless benefits should be gradually lowered to boost active job hunting by the unemployed. Another proposal was to expand the use of reduced VAT in labour-intensive service industries.
The group underlined that their report's proposals would work towards a substantial upturn in jobs creation only if all measures were implemented -- not just the pleasant ones.
